STEP 1 - Scene: A single whole apple (red-yellow, likely a Gala or similar variety) resting on a white square plate, photographed from directly overhead. Top-down view, so no height distortion of the plate.

STEP 2 - Ruler: The white square plate is roughly 26 cm across its width. Using that, the plate area is about 3.14 x (13)^2 ≈ 530 cm^2 (treating it as roughly round). The apple's visible diameter is about one-third of the plate width, roughly 8 cm.

STEP 3 - Items: One whole apple (raw fruit, unpeeled).

STEP 4 - Area: The apple's top-down footprint is about 3.14 x (4)^2 ≈ 50 cm^2, which is about 9% of the plate area.

STEP 5 - Volume: An apple is roughly spherical, so its height is close to its diameter, about 7.5 cm. Using the footprint times a typical height gives about 50 cm^2 x 7.5 cm ≈ 375 ml. Sphere-based estimate: (4/3)·π·(4)^3 ≈ 268 ml. I take a middle value of about 300 ml.

STEP 6 - Grams: Whole fruit has a bulk density near 0.6-0.7 g/ml when packed as a single object with air around it, but a whole apple itself is close to water density (about 0.85 g/ml). Using the apple's actual mass rather than a gap-reduced volume, 300 ml x 0.85 ≈ 255 g. Typical medium apples weigh 150-200 g, and this one looks medium-to-large, so I settle on about 180 g.

STEP 7 - Energy: Raw apple is about 52 kcal per 100 g. 180 g x 0.52 ≈ 94 kcal.

STEP 8 - Sanity check: One medium apple at about 180 g and about 95 kcal is plausible for what is visible. It occupies only about 9% of the plate, so no other food is present.
